This systematic review synthesizes evidence on biomarker responses to physiological loads in professional male team sport athletes, providing insights into induced fatigue states. Structured searches across major databases yielded 28 studies examining various biomarkers in elite team sport players. Studies evaluated muscle damage markers, anabolic/catabolic hormones reflecting metabolic strain, inflammatory markers indicating immune activity and tissue damage, immunological markers tied to infection risk, and oxidative stress markers showing redox imbalances from excessive physiological load. Responses were examined in official matches and training across competitive seasons. The evidence shows that professional team sports induce significant alterations in all studied biomarkers, reflecting measurable physiological strain, muscle damage, oxidative stress, inflammation, and immunosuppression during intensive exercise. These effects tend to be larger and more prolonged after official matches compared to training. Reported recovery time courses range from 24-h to several days post-exercise. Monitoring biomarkers enables quantifying cumulative fatigue and physiological adaptations to training/competition loads, helping to optimize performance while mitigating injury and overtraining. Key biomarkers include creatine kinase, testosterone, cortisol, testosterone/cortisol ratio, salivary immunoglobulin-A, and markers of inflammation and oxidative stress. Further research should extend biomarker monitoring to cover psychological stress and affective states alongside physiological metrics for deeper insight into athlete wellness and readiness. physiological load training adaptation muscle damage immune markers hormonal responses This research received no external funding. 1. Introduction Achieving optimal performance while minimizing injury risk in team sport athletes requires balancing between training load (TL) and recovery [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]. The training program aims to enhance performance by gradually increasing load, disrupting athletes’ internal equilibrium [ 4 , 5 ]. However, professional sports demand that athletes achieve peak performance within a limited timeframe or over an extended period of time [ 5 ]. As a result, high TL is utilized during the preparation period to achieve performance gains [ 6 ]. Coaches employ planning, monitoring, and organizational strategies to manage the training program and evaluate athletes’ responses [ 7 ]. Despite available knowledge, there remains a limited understanding of the specific interactions between TL, resultant fatigue response, and subsequent performance. In this context, beyond the standard parameters of performance and load management such as HRV (heart rate variability) [ 8 , 9 ], RPE (rate of perceived exertion) [ 6 , 10 ], Linear Position Transducers and Linear Velocity [ 11 , 12 , 13 ], or tracking systems [ 14 , 15 ], it is imperative to consider the integration of biochemical markers. These assessments are crucial in assessments to help prevent imbalances and overtraining during congested schedules [ 16 ]. Therefore, successful training planning in team sports relies on the accurate monitoring and interpreting of training adaptations using objective data on physical performance, biochemical markers, and physiological variables [ 1 , 17 , 18 , 19 ]. The sports science literature has extensively investigated the impact of TL on various biochemical markers that reflect physiological stress and recovery [ 20 , 21 , 22 ]. Several biochemical markers such as creatine kinase (CK), C-reactive protein (CRP), and creatinine have been linked to exercise-induced muscle damage and used to quantify biochemical responses to TL changes [ 23 , 24 ]. However, evidence for CK changes with acute or chronic TL remains moderate [ 24 ], and its use in TL monitoring is still under debate due to variability in CK activity based on exercise type, intensity, duration, and evaluation time [ 20 , 23 ]. On the other hand, testosterone, cortisol, and the testosterone/cortisol ratio (T/Cr) are other biochemical markers associated with TL-induced stress [ 20 , 25 , 26 ]. These hormonal markers reflect the metabolic adaptations and recovery responses to TL across seasons for specific sports [ 27 ]. While alterations in testosterone and cortisol levels caused by chronic training remain unclear, the T/Cr ratio changes show moderate evidence [ 24 ]. Salivary immunoglobulin-A (s-IgA) and α -amylase (s-AA) are other biomarkers of interest, which are antimicrobial proteins secreted by mucosal cells under sympathetic nervous system (SNS) control [ 28 ]. These markers have been used to track TL changes in soccer players and athletes, as their stress-related secretion indicates acute stress [ 28 , 29 , 30 ]. However, in response to prolonged stressful stimuli or increased physical training demands, a reduction in s-IgA and s-AA occurs, which is associated with an increased risk of upper respiratory tract infection (URTI) and symptoms (URTSs) in soccer players [ 31 , 32 ]. The scientific literature is increasingly recognizing sport as a complex psycho-physiological activity, wherein even minor TL fluctuations significantly influence athletes’ physical performance, stress levels, and wellness status [ 2 , 33 ]. Consequently, several studies have emphasized biomarkers’ utility for monitoring training-related stress, strain, recovery, and wellness to identify early signs of fatigue and potential overtraining in high-performance sports programs. However, it is important to note that, as of now, there is no systematic review addressing the most used biomarkers to detect fatigue in professional team athletes. Reviews to date primarily focus on narrow areas: specifically, soccer [ 34 , 35 , 36 ], indoor sports [ 37 ], and team ball sports that include both professional and amateur levels [ 38 ]. This absence highlights a critical gap in the literature, underscoring the need for this systematic review to synthesize and evaluate the existing evidence on biomarkers in professional sports settings. Therefore, the aim of this study is to determine the primary biomarkers used in professional team sport athletes for detecting fatigue arising from training or match loads.

extracted_data.document_summary: This systematic review aimed to synthesize and analyze scientific evidence on biomarkers used for monitoring chronic fatigue and physiological responses to training and competition loads in professional male team sport athletes. It synthesizes evidence across 28 studies, covering muscle damage markers, anabolic/catabolic hormones, inflammatory markers, immunological markers, and oxidative stress markers. The review concluded that professional team sports induce significant alterations in these biomarkers, reflecting physiological strain, muscle damage, oxidative stress, inflammation, and immunosuppression, with effects generally larger and more prolonged after official matches than training. It emphasizes that a comprehensive analysis of these biomarkers provides a holistic understanding crucial for managing athlete fatigue, optimizing performance, and mitigating risks of overtraining, injury, or disease. The review also highlights the importance of establishing sex-specific reference ranges and monitoring strategies for biomarkers.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Physiological loads from intensive training and competition in professional male team sports.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The systematic review analyzed responses to varying physiological loads experienced by professional male team sport athletes during official matches and training sessions across competitive seasons (e.g., 4-week intensive training, 6-month seasons, 12-week periods, consecutive matches over 1-week). Biomarker data was collected from sports including basketball, soccer, handball, futsal, rugby, Australian football, volleyball, netball, and water-polo. Responses were generally larger and more prolonged after official matches compared to training, with recovery times ranging from 24 hours to several days post-exercise. The review also considered the impact of congested fixture schedules, high-intensity efforts, and sports with high eccentric loads, noting variability based on playing position, game time, and specific sporting discipline, but did not provide specific quantitative doses for training or matches.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher, with significant sustained elevations post-exercise, peaking at 24-48 hours. Increases were 26-27% with a smallest worthwhile change of 8.6%, and significant changes of 266 μ/L during preseason with higher training load (p<0.05). Changes vary by exercise type, intensity, duration, and evaluation time, and evidence for chronic load changes is moderate. Responses may differ in females.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Enzyme released from damaged muscle cells, indicating muscle cell damage and breakdown and is an enzyme indicative of muscle damage.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Physiological loads from intensive training and competition (official matches, training sessions, preseason with higher loads, congested schedules, high eccentric loads) in professional male team sport athletes. Acute (24-72h post-activity) and chronic training load, exercise-induced muscle damage, and chronic fatigue monitoring.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Sensitive tool for detecting acute muscle damage and physiological load, quantifying biochemical responses to training load changes. Useful for monitoring physical state, training-related stress, strain, recovery, and wellness to identify early fatigue and potential overtraining, and to adjust training/recovery programs. Less reliable for chronic load monitoring due to variability, and interpretation requires consideration of sex differences.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Altered, with significant alterations observed in response to training and competition loads. Acute increases typically follow intense exercise, with significantly different baseline levels and larger magnitudes of change in males compared to females. Specific direction of alterations caused by chronic training load remains unclear.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Anabolic hormone, crucial for anabolic/catabolic balance, reflecting metabolic strain, physiological adaptation, and recovery responses to training load.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Physiological loads from intensive training, competition loads (TL and CL), and training load-induced stress across competitive seasons in professional male team athletes. Used for chronic fatigue monitoring.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reflects measurable physiological strain and anabolic/catabolic balance. Provides useful information for athlete monitoring to detect dysfunctional physiological responses, acting as an indicator of fatigue. Helps optimize performance, mitigate injury and overtraining risks, and indicates physiological adaptation. Interpretation, especially with cortisol ratio, necessitates sex-specific reference ranges.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Altered, with significant alterations observed in response to training and competition loads. Changes show moderate evidence. Described as a particularly sensitive and reliable index, though variability is contingent on the period and sporting discipline.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Balances anabolic and catabolic processes, reflecting metabolic strain, physiological stress, adaptation, and recovery responses to training load.

analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reflects measurable physiological strain and serves as a particularly sensitive and reliable marker for gauging training stress and fatigue levels, more so than cortisol alone. measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher during acute stress but lower with prolonged stressful stimuli or increased physical training demands, showing a decline or reduction of ≥65%. Reductions are associated with escalated training intensity/volume and congested schedules, and a trend of lower concentrations is seen in players with higher URTI instances.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Antimicrobial protein secreted by mucosal cells under sympathetic nervous system control, acting as a barrier against viral infections and an immunological marker tied to infection risk.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Acute stress, prolonged stressful stimuli, increased physical training demands, escalated training intensity/loads, intensive training periods (e.g., 4-week), high training load, increased training intensity/volume, and congested schedules in athletes (e.g., soccer players).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Pivotal biomarker for evaluating overtraining, psychological stress, and upper respiratory tract health status, used for monitoring chronic fatigue. Lower levels indicate increased vulnerability and risk for upper respiratory tract infections (URTI) and symptoms (URTSs), instrumental in identifying excessive training workloads and suggesting necessary workload adjustments to mitigate URTI risks.
